opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I don't think there's a clean formula, but there are a few heuristics I keep coming back to.

The first is transfer. If I train on this domain jointly, does it make the rest of the model better, or at least not worse? Code is the classic example. People once treated it as a niche skill you might bolt on, but it improves reasoning, structured thinking, and long-horizon planning across the board. When a domain has that kind of positive spillover, it belongs inside the main model. You'd be leaving value on the table otherwise.

The second is whether the knowledge is really about understanding or about precision. A lot of what makes a world model powerful is that it builds rich, compressed representations of how things relate: physics intuitions, social dynamics, how a proof is shaped. But some things are fundamentally lookup or exact computation, like a database of current stock prices, a high-precision numerical solver, or a symbolic algebra engine. The model doesn't need to internalize those. It needs to know when to reach for them and how to interpret what comes back. Forcing the weights to memorize that stuff is inefficient and brittle.

The third is how fast the domain changes. If the information goes stale in weeks, baking it into pretraining is a losing game. You want retrieval or a tool there, and the model's job is judgment over fresh inputs.

Then there's a practical question about capacity and interference. Every domain you add competes for parameters and training compute. If something is very narrow and doesn't share structure with anything else, say some extremely specialized sensor format, it may dilute the model without much benefit. A separate expert is cleaner.

The general trend, though, has been that more things belong inside than people initially expect. Repeatedly, the bet that "this is too specialized, it needs its own system" has lost to the bet that a sufficiently large, well-trained general model picks it up and connects it to everything else. So my default prior leans toward joint training, and I want a fairly concrete reason, like precision, freshness, or real interference, before carving something out into a tool.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the honest answer is that it's an empirical question, and the default should be to try putting it in the joint model first, because the history of this field has mostly been one of joint training winning more often than people expected.

The way I tend to think about it is to ask what the domain shares with everything else the model already knows. If a new domain has structure that overlaps with language, with reasoning, with the kinds of abstractions the model already represents, then you're going to get transfer in both directions. The model gets better at the new thing because it already understands related things, and sometimes, which is the more surprising part, the existing capabilities get better because the new data forces the model to sharpen representations it was being lazy about. Code is the canonical example. People initially thought of code as a somewhat separate domain, and it turned out to be one of the most important ingredients for general reasoning.

Where I'd lean toward a separate tool is when the domain is really governed by something the model fundamentally can't internalize well. Exact arithmetic over long numbers, or a database lookup, or anything where the ground truth is changing in real time. There the failure mode of joint training is that you're spending enormous capacity and compute to approximate something a calculator does perfectly for free. And the model will hallucinate in exactly the way you don't want, confidently and fluently. So the question I ask is, is this knowledge or is this a procedure with a crisp correct answer? Knowledge tends to want to live in the weights. Crisp procedures with external state tend to want to be tools.

But there's a subtlety, which is that even when you decide something is a tool, the model still needs to learn when and how to use it, and that judgment absolutely belongs in the joint model. So it's rarely a clean either-or. You usually end up with the world model holding the understanding of the domain and the tool holding the precise execution.

And the thing I'd caution people against is deciding too early. The cost of being wrong in the direction of "we'll bolt it on as a tool" is that you never discover the transfer you would have gotten, and that's invisible to you. The cost of being wrong in the other direction is usually measurable, you see the model being bad at it, and you can walk it back. So I'd rather err toward joint training and let the evaluation tell me I was wrong.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much that domain benefits from sharing representations with everything else. If learning it helps the model reason about other domains, and knowledge from other domains helps it in return, that’s a strong argument for joint training.

But there are capabilities where you really want a separate tool. A calculator is the obvious example: you want an exact answer, and there’s a very reliable procedure for getting it. Similarly, if information changes frequently, retrieving it may make more sense than trying to keep it all in the model’s weights.

And those aren’t mutually exclusive. You want the model to understand enough mathematics to formulate the right calculation and interpret the result, even if it delegates the arithmetic. So I’d look at transfer, reliability, and the cost of keeping the capability up to date. Then I’d test whether integrating it actually improves the overall system. I don’t think there’s a clean boundary you can determine in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much that domain benefits from sharing representations with everything else. If learning it helps the model reason more broadly, or if understanding it requires a lot of context from other domains, then there’s a strong case for joint training. You want the model to be able to bring those pieces together without having to specify an interface between them in advance.

But there are also things where a separate tool is a very natural fit. A calculator is the obvious example: you have a well-defined operation, you can execute it reliably, and you can check the result. There’s less reason to force the model to implement that operation internally every time.

And I don’t think that’s a clean binary. The model needs enough understanding of a domain to know when to call the expert, what question to ask, and whether the answer makes sense. So I’d look at the marginal benefit of putting more of that capability into the shared model: does it improve transfer and reasoning enough to justify the training cost, or are you better off improving the tool and the model’s ability to use it?
